runs.text: Short answer: the documents do not say whether a battery passport is feasible in India. None of the papers discusses India's market, policy, recyclers or infrastructure. The only place the word India appears is an author's affiliation, which is not a discussion of the topic:

.

The only passport paper in the set is the Materials Today review on recycling (mattod-2020). It proposes the Battery Identity Global Passport (BIGP) as a concept:

support.quote: introduced as the Battery Identity Global Passport (BIGP)
through a digital chip comprising information that identifies

runs.text: the battery at manufacture and at recycling. The review's own schematic is labelled

support.quote: (a) Schematic of Battery Identity Global Passport (BIGP)

runs.text:
.

The review presents the passport as an idea that still needs to be built and agreed. It says

support.quote: Obviously, such a concept will have to be globally

runs.text: implemented, because otherwise the global battery flow may jeopardize recycling. It also notes that sharing data is hard, because

support.quote: manufacturers may not want to share their proprietary

runs.text: formulations, so stakeholders and policymakers would need to make agreements. It cites a World Economic Forum and Global Battery Alliance view that

support.quote: systems or battery passports should be established, especially for

runs.text:
EV batteries.

So the papers support the passport as a global concept that is desirable and needs cross-border agreement. They do not show that it is practical in India. Answering that would need Indian-specific evidence, such as the country's battery recycling capacity, regulation and data systems, which these documents do not contain.
